evidence: Cic. Leg. 3.30: sīc ēmendārī et corrigī continentiā
terms.comment: To free from faults (mendum, a fault): a state, laws, habits; its commonest use is correcting a text or a speech, and in Pliny the Elder curing a complaint (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Leg. 3.32: vel corrumpere mōrēs cīvitātis vel corrigere
Plaut. Trin. 1.2.81: ad frūgem corrigere (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To make straight, and far more often to set right: a person, morals, a mistake; Cicero pairs it with ēmendāre (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: a reform, an amendment, a correction
evidence: Cic. Fin. 4.21: corrēctiō et ēmendātiō philosophiae veteris (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The noun for a reform; corrēctiō is used beside it (Lewis & Short).
Not before Augustus: first to reshape, transform (Ovid), then to reform a person or morals (Seneca, Pliny). Morgan–Owens records reformātiō agrāria for land reform, from a modern concordat.

phrases.latin: cum tot sustineās et tanta negōtia sōlus, rēs Ītalās armīs tūtēris, mōribus ōrnēs, lēgibus ēmendēs
phrases.english: since you alone carry so many and such great burdens, guarding Italy with arms, gracing her with morals, reforming her with laws

phrases.latin: ut enim cupiditātibus prīncipum et vitiīs īnficī solet tōta cīvitās, sīc ēmendārī et corrigī continentiā
phrases.english: for as a whole state is usually infected by the greed and vices of its leading men, so it is reformed and set right by their self-restraint
